system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2172-07-18 05:19:00 to 2172-07-20 19:02:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a severe frontal headache, fever, and elevated white blood cell count. The headache responded well to Imitrex, supporting a diagnosis of migraine, though initial concern for meningitis led to empiric antibiotics, later discontinued. She was found to have cellulitis in the left lower leg and a urinary tract infection caused by E. coli, both treated with appropriate antibiotics. Her INR was elevated on admission, so Coumadin was held and later restarted at discharge. HIV medications were resumed, and she was discharged home with instructions to complete antibiotics, monitor INR, and follow up on pending lab results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___ and I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in with some urinary symptoms and fatigue—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had burning when I pee and going a lot more often. It’s been like that for three days. I’ve also been really tired and coughing more than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned some chest pain with the cough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sharp pain when I breathe deep. And I’ve had this sore on my buttock for two weeks. It’s not healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We also noticed you haven’t been able to keep your medications down because of nausea. That includes your Coumadin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I just couldn’t keep anything down. I was so nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on antibiotics because your urine test was very positive for infection. You got a dose of gentamicin in the ER, and we’ll switch to an oral antibiotic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it another UTI like before? I get them a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very likely. And we’re watching for ESBL, a type of resistant E. coli you’ve had before. We’ll confirm with the culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about my kidneys. I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function looked okay at first—creatinine was 0.9. But we’ll keep an eye on it, especially since you haven’t been eating or drinking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds? I didn’t take them the last few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your HIV medications. Your viral load is undetectable and CD4 is strong—over 1000—so that’s excellent. We want to keep it that way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about the sore on my butt? It’s painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a stage II pressure ulcer. We’ve started moist wound dressings to help it heal. A nurse will change it daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using a powder for the rash under my skin folds. I ran out at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted you have intertriginous candidiasis. We’re continuing the miconazole powder three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel like I can’t care for myself at home anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware. There are concerns about your caretaker. Social work is helping set up home services for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think she’s stealing from me. I don’t trust her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through that. The team is working to get you support so you can stay safe at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. It’s ESBL E. coli, sensitive to Bactrim, which is what we’re using. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotic is working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s the right choice. But we noticed your creatinine went up to 1.4 yesterday. That means your kidneys were a bit stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely because you weren’t eating or drinking much before admission. Your blood was a bit thick—hematocrit was high. We started IV fluids, and your creatinine is already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not permanent damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like temporary, or ‘pre-renal,’ kidney issue. It’s responding well. Your latest creatinine is 0.7—back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my breathing? I still have crackles in my lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray showed atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—likely from shallow breathing due to pain or weakness. It’s not pneumonia. We’re encouraging deep breathing and your inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been using my Symbicort. I forgot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted it. It’s important for your asthma. We’ll make sure you have it at discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a kidney ultrasound yesterday to check for stones. Good news—it shows no stones or blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had stones before. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs now. Your kidneys look structurally normal. That supports our view that the kidney issue was due to dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’ll finish the Bactrim for 11 more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my Coumadin? I was taking different doses on different days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re simplifying it to 10 mg daily. You’ll need to follow up with your anticoagulation clinic tomorrow to check your INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my wound care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the moist dressings daily. Home health will visit to help. And keep using the antifungal powder for your skin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I’m getting help at home. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re setting you up with services to prevent that. Keep taking all your meds, especially for HIV and heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve made great progress. We’ll see you in follow-up, and call if anything changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with dysuria, urinary frequency, fatigue, and a stage II pressure ulcer, with concerns about her ability to care for herself at home. She was diagnosed with a UTI caused by ESBL-producing E. coli, which was treated with Bactrim after an initial IV dose of gentamicin. Her creatinine rose to 1.4, likely due to pre-renal azotemia from poor oral intake, but improved with IV fluids and returned to baseline. A kidney ultrasound showed no stones or structural issues. Her HIV remained well-controlled with undetectable viral load, and her pressure ulcer and intertriginous candidiasis were managed with appropriate wound care and topical antifungal. Social work addressed concerns about caregiver abuse, and home health services were arranged. She was discharged home with simplified warfarin dosing and instructions to complete antibiotics and follow up with her anticoagulation clinic.
